p.x:
Last Saturday, I went to watch the football final with my dad. Our team was playing against the best team in the country. We are big fans, so we wore red shirts and took a flag.
The stadium was full. Before the match, everyone stood up and sang. When the players came out, the fans started to clap and shout. In the first half, nobody scored. Then, in the second half, our captain kicked the ball into the net. Goal! Everyone cheered.
Ten minutes later, the other team scored. But just before the end, our young player beat two defenders and scored again. We won 2–1! At the end, the captain lifted the gold trophy, and the players threw their shirts to the fans. It was the best day of my life.

The Olympic Games are the biggest sports event in the world. Every four years, a different city hosts the Summer Games, and more than 10,000 athletes take part. To compete, athletes must first qualify by reaching a certain standard in their sport.
The winners of each event receive medals: gold for first place, silver for second and bronze for third. They stand on the podium while the national anthem of the winner's country is played. For many athletes, it is the greatest moment of their lives.
Some of the most popular events take place in the athletics stadium. The 100-metre sprint, which lasts less than ten seconds, decides 'the fastest person on Earth'. In the relay, four runners from each country pass a baton to each other. In longer races, the runners must complete many laps of the track. The marathon, which goes through the streets of the host city, ends the Games.
The Games also have a mascot, often a friendly animal, which appears on souvenirs. Each venue is full of fans, and each victory brings joy to a whole country. Many athletes also dream of breaking a world record.

When a city wins its bid to host the Olympic Games or the World Cup, celebrations often fill the streets. Hosting such an event promises international prestige, a boost to tourism and a sense of national pride. Few spectacles unite a country like a home victory in a knockout match, with crowds singing the anthem in a wave of patriotic emotion.
Yet the economic reality is frequently disappointing. Budgets regularly double or triple, and cities are left with enormous debts. After the 2004 Athens Olympics, several expensive venues stood empty for years, becoming classic examples of white elephants. Construction has also displaced residents: in some host cities, thousands of families were moved from their homes to make way for stadiums.
Controversy is not limited to money. Some events have been marked by political boycotts, while others have been criticised for the treatment of migrant workers or for awarding hosting rights to countries with poor human-rights records.
Organisers point out that the events themselves are lucrative for sports bodies, mainly through broadcasting and sponsorship deals. The challenge is to ensure that host cities share the benefits. Recent bids have therefore focused on reusing existing facilities and planning a positive legacy, such as new public transport or affordable housing. Whether mega-events can become genuinely sustainable remains to be seen, and some critics argue that the penalty for poor planning is still paid by ordinary residents rather than by organisers.
